body.text: When the French soccer star Kylian Mbappe last week issued an apology for his remark about a “Chinese dictator,” he didn’t mince his words: “I have deep respect for the Chinese people and their history, and I am sincerely sorry.” Mbappe’s apology followed the latest instance of what has been termed China’s “emotional assertiveness” – a discursive practice whereby Chinese state representatives publicly invoke indignation on behalf of the Chinese population to pressure an alleged offender into acknowledging and respecting China’s red lines, thereby deterring others from violating them.

A long list of Western companies and celebrities have, sometimes preemptively, offered similar words of repentance to China over the past decade. Others have stood their ground, refusing to apologize despite intense pressure from Chinese government representatives.

What was interesting about the Mbappe incident was not so much the specific red line that was crossed by ridiculing China’s political leadership. Previous instances have been triggered by what the Chinese see as racial stereotypes (e.g. of Chinese tourists), seditious statements (e.g. in support of Hong Kong), smear campaigns (e.g. against Xinjiang) or distorted views (e.g. of Taiwan’s political status); it was only a matter of time before mockery of China’s leaders was added to the list.

Rather, the Mbappe incident stands out because of the entirely apolitical context of his alleged offense and the strikingly disproportionate response from China. Indeed, the fact that the highly influential French striker – himself nicknamed “the dictator” and playfully superimposed onto historical dictators in social media memes – was oblivious to Mao and did not even mention his name in the controversial interview should have tempered the emotional response in China.

Instead, the Chinese government resorted to a full-throated campaign of emotional assertiveness. As the spokesperson of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs made clear, “any rhetoric or action that hurts the feelings of the Chinese people will naturally be rejected across the sectors in China.”

Meanwhile, the Chinese government deployed its many levers to orchestrate and intensify the pressure. Several Chinese companies immediately announced the termination of their sponsor contracts with Mbappe. Chinese state television threatened to suspend its broadcasts of La Liga, while the Global Times and China Daily tightened the screws on Mbappe’s club, Real Madrid, which is sponsored by China’s consumer electronics giant Hisense. In the end, not only Mbappe, but also La Liga and Real Madrid succumbed to the pressure, with all three of them issuing separate apologies.
As things have cooled down, we are left with uncomfortable questions about both the seemingly expansive nature of China’s emotional sensitivities and the growing reach of its influence and power.

Will all Western celebrities, companies, and perhaps even media have to toe Beijing’s red lines, or risk being targeted directly by the full force of the party-state for offending the national sentiments of the Chinese population? Will China’s indispensable position in global supply chains, its growing command over critical technologies and the continued allure of its market ultimately compel Western governments to respect these red lines as well? And will, one might add, the United States’ abdication of its traditional role as a champion of liberal values allow the Chinese government to police its red lines more aggressively?

So far, the only Western non-state actors to have weathered the storm of China’s emotional assertiveness have been media organizations: Swedish National Television in 2018 following a comedy skit ridiculing Chinese tourists; Danish newspaper Jyllands-Posten in 2020 over a satirical drawing of the Chinese flag featuring corona virus symbols; and the Wall Street Journal in 2020 for publishing an op-ed entitled “China is the real sick man of Asia.” While all three media organizations offered some sort of conciliatory gesture or expression of understanding, none of them offered what the Chinese would consider a “sincere apology.”

To be sure, the absence of commercial interests in China and their commitment to freedom of expression principles go a long way toward explaining the steadfastness of these media in the face of intense pressure from the Chinese government. Yet we should not underestimate the deterrent effect of China’s emotional assertiveness and how it may prompt others to self-censor. Indeed, Western media appear not to have crossed China’s red lines since the controversy over the WSJ headline.

Mbappe himself may have been completely unaware of having crossed one of China’s red lines. But Beijing seems intent on teaching him – and the rest of us – how to respect China’s national sentiments. Whatever that means.
